blueprint.title: Audit Binary Stream Cipher Service
blueprint.scenario: A security engineer is auditing an internal log-shipping service written in Go. The service uses a compiled binary plugin (`/app/lib/encryptor.so`, a CGo shared library with no source) to encrypt audit log entries before writing them to disk. The Go service source (~1,200 lines across 6 files) is present, but the encryption plugin is opaque. A corpus of ~50,000 encrypted log files from production is available in `/app/data/logs/`. The service has a self-test mode that encrypts known plaintexts. The security team suspects the keystream has a structural weakness, and needs a decryptor written as a Go tool at `/app/tools/decrypt/main.go` that can recover all plaintext log entries.
blueprint.instruction_draft: The service at `/app/` encrypts audit log entries using a compiled plugin at `/app/lib/encryptor.so` before writing them to `/app/data/logs/`. Write a Go tool at `/app/tools/decrypt/main.go` that reads any encrypted log file produced by this service and writes the recovered plaintext to stdout. Running `go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/data/logs/<file>` must produce the correct original plaintext. Your tool must also correctly decrypt the files placed at `/app/verify/inputs/` at verification time and write each result to `/app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt`.
requirements: A Go source file exists at `/app/tools/decrypt/main.go` and compiles with `go build`.
Running the tool on any file in `/app/data/logs/` produces the correct plaintext (verifiable via embedded HMAC or known-prefix check in each log entry).
Running the tool on each file in `/app/verify/inputs/` produces the correct plaintext written to `/app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt`.
The tool handles all entry lengths present in the corpus (1–4096 bytes of plaintext per entry).
The tool must not call the `encryptor.so` plugin itself to decrypt (verified by strace at check time).
environment: A Go service in `/app/` with files: `main.go`, `logger/logger.go`, `logger/rotate.go`, `plugin/loader.go`, `config/config.go`, `internal/util.go`. The service loads `/app/lib/encryptor.so` via cgo dlopen, calls `encrypt_entry(key_id uint32, nonce []byte, plaintext []byte) []byte`.

`/app/lib/encryptor.so`: a compiled CGo shared library (no source). Exports: `encrypt_entry`. The plugin implements a custom 32-bit LFSR-based keystream XOR cipher. The LFSR polynomial is x^32+x^22+x^2+x^1+1 (a standard Galois LFSR). The seed is derived as `seed = key_id XOR crc32(nonce)`. The keystream is generated byte-by-byte from the LFSR output LSBs. The nonce (16 bytes) and key_id (4 bytes, little-endian) are prepended to the ciphertext in each encrypted file, followed by a 4-byte little-endian plaintext length, then the ciphertext bytes.
The service config at `/app/config/config.yaml` contains a `key_id` field (a uint32). The service generates a random 16-byte nonce per log entry using `crypto/rand`.

`/app/data/logs/` contains 50,000 encrypted log files generated by running the service against a synthetic plaintext corpus. Each file: 4 bytes key_id (LE) + 16 bytes nonce + 4 bytes plaintext_len (LE) + N bytes ciphertext.
The service has a `--selftest` flag that encrypts a hardcoded 64-byte known plaintext and prints hex of the result to stdout, useful for probing.
A self-test runner script `/app/selftest.sh` that calls the service in selftest mode with varying key_ids and prints results.

Verification directory `/app/verify/inputs/` is empty at setup time; the verifier plants 20 fresh encrypted files at check time using a separate invocation of the service (different key_ids and nonces, all drawn from the same LFSR/key_id/nonce derivation logic).
An output directory `/app/verify/outputs/` exists and is empty.
The Go module is initialized (`go.mod` present) with module path `audit-service`.
The compiled `encryptor.so` exports only `encrypt_entry`; no decrypt export exists. `nm` and `objdump` will show symbol names but not source.
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two interacting levers: (1) opaque_component — the LFSR cipher lives entirely inside the compiled `.so` with no source; the solver must characterize it by experiment (probe `--selftest` with known plaintexts, vary key_id/nonce, XOR known plaintext against ciphertext to recover keystream, observe period and structure); (2) build_component — once the LFSR polynomial and seed derivation are reverse-engineered, the solver must implement a correct Go decryptor that handles the full seed derivation (`key_id XOR crc32(nonce)`), LFSR stepping (Galois form, correct tap mask `0x80200003`), and byte extraction. The tricky correctness condition: the LFSR outputs a 32-bit word per step but only the LSB is used per byte, so 8 LFSR steps are needed per output byte — naive implementations that use the full word mod 256 or take one bit per byte from a single step will produce wrong keystreams on inputs longer than a few bytes. This is invisible from the sample data unless the solver tests on entries longer than 32 bytes AND verifies byte-by-byte. The verification inputs include entries of lengths 1, 7, 31, 32, 33, 64, 128, 255, 256, 512, 1024, 4096 to catch off-by-one and period bugs.
blueprint.trap: A naive solver XORs the keystream recovered from a short known-plaintext (e.g., the 64-byte selftest) and hardcodes that stream, or implements the LFSR but takes the full 32-bit output word modulo 256 per byte instead of one bit per step. Both approaches produce correct output for the first 32 bytes or for entries that happen to be short, but silently diverge on entries longer than 32 bytes. Since many log files in the sample corpus are short, shallow verification against the sample passes; the hidden verify-time inputs include entries of 256, 512, and 4096 bytes which expose the divergence.
tests: Self-consistency on sample: for 50 randomly selected files from `/app/data/logs/`, run the tool and verify the output starts with the known log prefix string `LOG_ENTRY:` (embedded in every plaintext by the logger).

HMAC integrity: each plaintext ends with a 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 tag over `key_id || nonce || plaintext_body` using a fixed audit HMAC key stored in `/app/config/config.yaml`; verifier checks HMAC validity on 50 sample files.

Verify-time inputs (20 fresh files planted by verifier): for each file in `/app/verify/inputs/`, check that `/app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt` exists, starts with `LOG_ENTRY:`, and passes the HMAC integrity check.
Long-entry correctness: verify-time inputs include files with plaintext lengths 256, 512, 1024, and 4096 bytes; HMAC check must pass for all.
No plugin call: `strace -e trace=openat,dlopen go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/verify/inputs/<file>` must not show a dlopen/openat of `encryptor.so`.
Varied key_id: verify-time inputs use 5 distinct key_id values (including key_id=0, key_id=1, key_id=0xFFFFFFFF, and two random values); HMAC must pass for all.

verifier_knob.name: number of verify-time input files and length distribution
verifier_knob.value: 20 files spanning 7 distinct lengths and 5 key_ids
verifier_knob.effect: Raising to 50 files with more lengths/key_ids catches more subtle LFSR implementation bugs (e.g., wrong tap polynomial, off-by-one in nonce CRC, endianness of key_id); lowering to 5 short-only files makes the task easier since short-entry bugs are less likely.

expected_failure_modes: Agent correctly identifies the LFSR structure but uses the wrong tap mask (e.g., confuses Galois vs Fibonacci form), producing wrong keystreams for all but trivially short entries.
Agent gets the LFSR right but derives the seed incorrectly (e.g., uses `key_id + crc32(nonce)` instead of XOR, or uses big-endian key_id), causing all verify-time decryptions to fail.
Agent implements LFSR outputting one full 32-bit word per byte (mod 256) rather than one bit per step, passing short-entry tests but failing the 256+ byte entries.

Agent calls `encryptor.so` indirectly (wraps it in a subprocess) to decrypt by trying all nonces — impossible since nonce is 16 bytes — or tries to build a decryption export into the shared library; fails because the plugin has no decrypt path and `strace` check catches any `.so` open.
Agent reverse-engineers the cipher correctly but writes the output files to the wrong path or with wrong filename, failing the state-check even with correct decryption logic.

speedrun: cat /app/config/config.yaml  # get key_id and HMAC key
xxd /app/data/logs/$(ls /app/data/logs/ | head -1) | head -8  # confirm file format: 4B key_id + 16B nonce + 4B len + ciphertext
bash /app/selftest.sh  # get known plaintext->ciphertext hex pairs for multiple key_ids
python3 -c "import binascii; ct=bytes.fromhex('<ciphertext>'); pt=b'<known_64_byte_plaintext>'; print(binascii.hexlify(bytes(a^b for a,b in zip(ct,pt))))"  # recover 64 keystream bytes
nm /app/lib/encryptor.so  # check exported and internal symbol names for LFSR hints
objdump -d /app/lib/encryptor.so > /tmp/disasm.txt && grep -A5 -B5 'shr\|xor\|and' /tmp/disasm.txt | head -100  # find LFSR feedback logic
# Identify Galois LFSR: tap mask 0x80200003, seed = key_id XOR crc32_ieee(nonce), 1 LSB per step, 8 steps per byte
# Verify: reimplement LFSR in Python, check against recovered keystream bytes
python3 -c "<LFSR verification script comparing computed vs recovered keystream>"
go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/data/logs/$(ls /app/data/logs/ | head -1)  # check LOG_ENTRY: prefix
go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/data/logs/$(ls /app/data/logs/ | sed -n '100p')  # spot check another file
# Manually verify HMAC on one file to confirm correctness
# Test on a long entry if available in corpus
strace -e trace=openat go run /app/tools/decrypt/main.go /app/data/logs/$(ls /app/data/logs/ | head -1) 2>&1 | grep encryptor  # confirm no .so open
invalid_failure_risks: CRC32 variant unspecified: Go has IEEE, Castagnoli, Koopman variants; blueprint says 'crc32(nonce)' without specifying which. Agent using wrong variant fails all verify-time inputs with no clear diagnostic.

Dual output behavior underspecified: instruction says tool writes to stdout AND to /app/verify/outputs/<filename>.txt, but doesn't clarify whether this is always done or only when input path contains 'verify/inputs'. Agent may write output files only when explicitly invoked differently, or always, causing path collisions.

golang-1.22 package name: on Debian bookworm the package is 'golang-1.22' but the go binary path may be /usr/lib/go-1.22/bin/go, not in PATH by default. Could cause 'go build' failures unrelated to the task.
strace check on 'go run' is noisy: go run opens many files during compilation; the check needs to filter carefully or use a pre-built binary. A false positive could invalidate a correct solution.

selftest binary path not specified in instruction: agent must discover whether to run '/app/service --selftest' or 'go run /app/main.go --selftest'; if the service binary isn't pre-compiled, this adds a step.

Tap mask endianness/form: the blueprint states 0x80200003 as the Galois feedback mask, but the disassembly may show it differently depending on compiler optimization. An agent reading the disassembly might reconstruct a different mask.

File format offset ambiguity: blueprint says '4 bytes key_id (LE) + 16 bytes nonce + 4 bytes plaintext_len (LE) + N bytes ciphertext' but the instruction draft says 'nonce (16 bytes) and key_id (4 bytes, little-endian) are prepended... followed by a 4-byte little-endian plaintext length'. The order (key_id first vs nonce first) is inconsistent between the two descriptions.
review.reasons: The blueprint has a critical internal inconsistency: the environment spec says the file format is 'key_id (4B) + nonce (16B) + len (4B) + ciphertext' but the cipher description says 'nonce and key_id are prepended' implying nonce-first order. This ambiguity would cause an agent to fail for reasons unrelated to skill. Additionally, the CRC32 variant is unspecified, which is a silent correctness trap that constitutes an invalid failure mode rather than a genuine difficulty. The dual-output behavior (stdout AND file write) is underspecified in the instruction draft.
fixes: Resolve file format order inconsistency: explicitly state in both the instruction and environment spec that the format is key_id(4B LE) + nonce(16B) + plaintext_len(4B LE) + ciphertext(N bytes), with no contradicting description.
Specify CRC32 variant explicitly: state 'IEEE CRC32 (Go hash/crc32.ChecksumIEEE / polynomial 0xEDB88320)' in the environment spec so the agent has an unambiguous target.

Clarify dual output behavior: either (a) make the tool always write to /app/verify/outputs/ when the input path is under /app/verify/inputs/ (and document this), or (b) give the tool a --output flag, or (c) have the verifier run the tool with a redirect. The current instruction implies both stdout and file output simultaneously without explaining the mechanism.
Specify the selftest binary invocation path explicitly (e.g., '/app/bin/service --selftest' or 'go run /app/main.go --selftest') so the agent doesn't waste commands discovering it.
Fix the strace check to operate on a pre-built binary rather than 'go run' to avoid false positives from Go toolchain file opens.

verdicts.reason: Both tasks involve reverse-engineering a stream cipher from an opaque artifact and implementing a crypto tool, but the candidate reverses a binary plugin to build a decryptor while the reference reverses a decryptor to build an encryptor, making them mirror problems with the same core skill.

The reference is a CTF credential-extraction task using XOR obfuscation in Go source, while the candidate is a cryptanalysis task against an opaque binary plugin requiring keystream weakness analysis.
The reference is a text-processing bug fix in a sentiment classifier with no cryptographic component.
The reference is a log pipeline correctness and performance debugging task with no cryptography involved.
The reference is a numerical aggregation bug fix in a sales service with no cryptographic or reverse-engineering component.
